div.p: For people living in Quebec, with notes for the rest of Canada. Every fact comes from an official source, listed at the end and read on October 2, 2026. Rules and phone numbers change: check the source before you act.
This app does not connect to Equifax or TransUnion and stores no credit data. Your reminders are visible to you only. This guide gives general information; it is not legal advice.

Your credit file (also called credit report) is your credit history: your identity, your loans and cards and how you repay them, your bank accounts and NSF cheques, unpaid accounts, public records (bankruptcy, judgment), who asked to see your file, and your score (AMF).

Your credit score is a number between 300 and 900 computed from the file; the higher, the better. There is no single score: lenders receive other scores than the one you get, but they tend toward the same value (AMF). Scores are updated at least once a month (FCAC).
Checking your own file or score has no effect on your score (FCAC).

In Quebec, the law gives you the right to get your score with the explanations needed to understand it, notably online, free of charge, and free online access to your file (Credit Assessment Agents Act, ss. 13, 15 and 46).
Each bureau keeps its own file, and a measure placed with one does not apply to the other (Equifax, TransUnion).

ul.li: Equifax: online with a my.equifax.ca account, free, updated monthly; Equifax says this data is stored in the United States. By phone: 1-800-465-7166 (automated, asks for your SIN; mailed in 5 to 10 days). By mail: the request form with copies of two valid government ID, one showing your current address, to Equifax Canada, Relations nationales avec les consommateurs, C. P. 190, Montréal (Québec) H1S 2Z2.

TransUnion: online at ocs.transunion.ca, a free consumer disclosure every month; for Quebec and Ontario residents it includes the score and its factors. By phone: 1-800-663-9980. By mail: the consumer request form with copies (front and back) of two ID that together show your name, current address, date of birth and signature, to TransUnion, Consumers Relations Department, 3115 Harvester Road, Suite 201, Burlington, ON L7N 3N8.
Online access is free and needs no credit card number. By mail, reasonable fees may be asked for sending the file (AMF).

div.h2: 3. How often, and what to check
div.p: At least once a year, and each time something looks suspicious: a bill for a service you never asked for, a collection agency calling about an unknown debt, a lender mentioning credit you never requested (AMF, CAI, FCAC). Your reminders alternate the two bureaus every six months.
What to check (FCAC, AMF, TransUnion):

ul.li: errors in your personal information (address, date of birth);
errors in loans or credit cards, and late payments shown when you paid on time;
accounts you never opened: a possible sign of identity theft;

negative information still there after the maximum retention period; in Quebec, an agent must destroy information collected more than seven years ago (Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, s. 79.1);
who consulted your file, and at TransUnion the blocked requests while a freeze is on: contact any company you do not know.

div.p: To fix an error, write to the bureau (each has a dispute form). It must answer within 30 days; without an answer, the request is deemed refused. You can then ask the Commission d'accès à l'information to examine the disagreement, within 30 days (private sector act, s. 32; CAI).
div.h2: 4. Quebec: your rights under the Credit Assessment Agents Act
div.p: In force since February 1, 2021; the security freeze applies since February 1, 2023 (Quebec Department of Finance). Three protective measures, each can be revoked; the freeze can also be suspended (s. 8).

ul.li: Security freeze (s. 9): the bureau may not share your file to open credit, raise a credit limit, sign a long-term lease of goods (a car lease, for example) or a remote service contract (a cell phone plan, for example). Employers, collection agencies, governments, landlords and insurers can still see the file with your permission (AMF).

Security alert (s. 10): whoever receives your file must take reasonable steps to make sure it is really you before contracting, and gets the phone number you gave, which the request must include (s. 19; private sector act, s. 19.1).
Explanatory note (ss. 11 and 20): your side of a disagreement with the bureau on access to or correction of your file; it describes the disagreement and must not be defamatory.

div.p: Costs. Every right is free, except the freeze, for which the law allows reasonable fees (ss. 15 and 18). In practice the freeze is free in Quebec (AMF), and neither bureau charges for it (Equifax, TransUnion). Using a right cannot lower your score (s. 16).

How. The request comes from you (or your representative), with proof of identity; it can be made orally, except for an explanatory note (s. 17). The bureau must agree to a compliant request and answer in writing, with its reasons and your recourses if it refuses (ss. 21 and 22). Online: from your Equifax or TransUnion account (AMF).

Delays. The law refers to a delay set by government regulation (ss. 22 and 23); none of the three regulations under the Act sets it (LégisQuébec, up to date June 10, 2026). The bureaus announce: Equifax, immediate online or by phone, up to five business days by mail; TransUnion, immediate online or by phone, up to 30 days by mail.

Duration. The law sets none: a measure ends when you revoke it (s. 12). A freeze stays until you lift it (Equifax, TransUnion). An alert stays six years at Equifax and at TransUnion: your reminders plan its renewal. To change the phone number of an Equifax alert, write with proof of identity and a phone bill.

Applying for credit with a freeze. Lift it at both bureaus first. Equifax lets you suspend the lock for a period, then locks again by itself. At TransUnion, a suspension with an end date is announced from July 1, 2027; until then a lifted freeze is not restored automatically: add a reminder to put it back.

Recourse. If the bureau refuses: ask the Commission d'accès à l'information to examine the disagreement (s. 24). If it does not answer in time or does not follow through: complain to the Autorité des marchés financiers, 1-877-525-0337 (s. 25; AMF).

ul.li: Review your credit card statement every month and report an unknown transaction to the issuer right away (FCAC); watch bank and card statements and any new bill in the mail (AMF).
Be wary of opened envelopes and of statements that stop arriving (Service Canada).
A federally regulated bank must alert you when available credit or a balance falls below $100 or an amount you set (FCAC). These alerts help manage balances; they are not fraud alerts.
Credit monitoring services from the bureaus are paid and do not include the security alert (AMF). After a breach, ask whether your bank, credit union or insurer offers monitoring for free (AMF).

Lost or stolen credit card: tell the issuer without delay. After that notice you owe nothing for a third party's use; even without notice, your liability is limited to $50 (Consumer Protection Act, s. 123).
a creditor reports a credit application made with your name and SIN;
calls or letters about credit you never applied for;
bills for services you never ordered;
statements or mail that stop arriving;
unknown purchases on a statement;
a collection agency chasing a debt from an account you never opened;
an unknown account in your credit file.

div.p: Sources: TransUnion, AMF, FCAC, Service Canada.

ol.li: Call your financial institutions and card issuers; close compromised accounts and ask for a warning note on your accounts (CAI, Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre).
Change your passwords, from another device if the fraudster had access to yours (AMF).
Report it to the police and get a file number (Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre). In Quebec: the Sûreté du Québec or your municipal police (AMF).

Freeze your file at Equifax and at TransUnion, or add a fraud alert, or both (CAI, AMF). Equifax 1-800-465-7166, TransUnion 1-800-663-9980. TransUnion charges $5 plus taxes for an alert through its automated phone line and nothing through other channels; in Quebec the alert is free by law (s. 15): use the website or write.
Report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre: online (anonymously if you wish) or 1-888-495-8501, Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. Eastern time.
Ask unknown creditors to close the accounts you did not open (Service Canada).

Social insurance number: you do not have to report SIN fraud to the SIN program. A new SIN is issued only with proof of fraudulent use and is not advised: the old one is not erased and stays your responsibility. If your SIN was used to get government money, report it to that program (Service Canada).

Lost or stolen ID: tell the issuer. Health insurance card (RAMQ): replace it online for $15 by credit card, or by mail for $25. Driver's licence: tell the SAAQ (CAI). Passport: Passport Canada and the police (Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre).
Also tell Revenu Québec and the Canada Revenue Agency, Canada Post if your mail is diverted, and your service providers (CAI, Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre).
Keep everything: timeline, documents, receipts, emails, texts, transfer proofs. Beware of a second scam promising to recover your money (AMF, Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre).

div.p: Help: the Office de la protection du consommateur when the theft involves a consumer product; the AMF for an investment product; the Université de Montréal cybercrime clinic, 438-901-4395, for victims of online fraud (AMF).

ul.li: The freeze is offered to residents of Quebec and Ontario only (Equifax, TransUnion). Ontario residents have it since July 1, 2026 (Equifax), free of charge; an alert there may cost up to $5 and expires after six years (Ontario government).
Elsewhere, a fraud alert remains possible; bureaus may ask for ID and charge fees (FCAC).
Score: free everywhere at Equifax; at TransUnion, free in Quebec and Ontario (FCAC).
The federal government does not regulate the bureaus: complain to the bureau first, then to your provincial or territorial consumer office (FCAC).
A different password for each account, at least 12 characters; a passphrase or a password manager helps (Québec.ca).
Turn on multi-factor authentication wherever it is offered (Get Cyber Safe, Québec.ca).

Phishing: do not open unexpected links or attachments; confirm an urgent request through another channel, with contact details you already have; report text-message phishing to 7726 (Get Cyber Safe, AMF).
Your SIN is not an ID: give it only when the law requires it. It is not needed to apply for a credit card, rent a home or get your credit report (Service Canada).
Shred personal papers before throwing them out (Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, CAI).
